transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's a bit of a story, honestly. I work as a personal care aide, you know, helping folks out, and we have these staff meetings. Important stuff, sure, but usually pretty dry. Anyway, we had one recently, and I don't know, I just... I got so incredibly worked up about the whole fall-prevention protocol. It's serious business, falls, you know? But I guess I took it a bit too far. I started actually acting out a whole drill right there in the middle of the room. I was pulling chairs around, setting up little obstacle courses, waving my arms everywhere to demonstrate how you're supposed to catch someone or clear the way. And the thing is... I just couldn't seem to stop. My supervisor, my coworkers, they were all telling me to sit down, saying "Okay, we get it, please take a seat," but I just kept going. It was like I was on a track and I couldn't get off it until the whole scene was finished. So, my boss thought maybe I should come talk to someone about it, and here I am.
Did you find yourself thinking about fall-prevention protocols repeatedly before that meeting?

No, not really. I mean, it's not like I was sitting at home obsessing over it or anything. It's just... well, fall prevention is part of the job, right? You always have to have it in the back of your mind when you're working with the elderly. You're always scanning the room, looking for loose rugs, making sure their walkers are within reach, checking if their shoes have good grip. It's second nature. But before the meeting? No, I wasn't dwelling on it. I was just going about my day, making my breakfast—I usually have oatmeal with a little brown sugar, sometimes some raisins if I have them—and taking the bus to work. I was actually thinking more about the weather because they said it was going to rain and I didn't want my clients slipping on the wet pavement. But the protocol itself? No, it wasn't stuck in my head or anything like that. It just sort of... erupted during the meeting. Like, once they brought it up on the agenda, it just clicked, and suddenly it felt like the most urgent, life-or-death thing in the world, and I just had to make sure everyone understood exactly how to handle it, down to the very last detail. But before that? No, not really.
Did your behavior during the meeting cause any problems for you at work or in your relationships with your coworkers?

Well, yes, actually, it caused a pretty big problem. It wasn't just a slap on the wrist or a "hey, calm down" kind of thing after the meeting ended. My supervisor pulled me into her office, and she looked really concerned, which honestly made me feel terrible because I've always prided myself on being reliable. She told me they were putting me on administrative leave from the senior center. Just like that. Paid leave, thankfully, but still... it's a shock to your system when you're told you can't come in to do the job you've been doing for years. I mean, I love my clients. Mr. Henderson relies on me for his morning walks, and Mrs. Gable won't let anyone else help her with her compression socks. So being told I can't be there... it's really been weighing on me. I've been sitting at home, just worrying constantly if I'm even going to be able to safely return to caregiving work at all. It's my livelihood, you know? 

And it's not just work, honestly. The whole thing has bled into everything else. My wife, Sarah, she's been a saint through all this, but I can tell it's taking a toll on her. I'm just... I'm not keeping up the way I used to. I'll start doing the dishes, and then I'll get sidetracked thinking about what happened, or just feeling completely drained, and the sink stays full. She's had to start reminding me about basic chores, like taking out the recycling on Tuesdays, and even my own appointments, like coming here today. I used to have all that locked down in my head. And church... well, we usually go every Sunday, and we have this little group we get coffee with afterward, but I've just been pulling back from them. I haven't gone the last two weeks. I just don't know what to say to them if they ask how work is going, and I don't want to explain the whole thing, so it's just easier to stay home. So, yeah, it's definitely caused a lot of problems, more than I ever expected from one staff meeting.
Have you ever felt a strong need to perform specific rituals or routines in your daily life, outside of work?

Rituals? Routines? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I have my habits, sure, but everyone has habits, right? Like I mentioned earlier, the oatmeal for breakfast—that's a habit, but it's not like a ritual where I have to stir it exactly ten times counterclockwise or something. It's just breakfast. And, you know, I always make sure the front door is locked before bed. That's just common sense, especially in our neighborhood. We had a string of car break-ins a few summers ago, just kids looking for loose change mostly, but it makes you aware. So I check the lock, maybe jiggle the handle once just to be sure, but it's not a compulsion. I don't stand there doing it over and over for twenty minutes. 

My wife, Sarah, she's actually the one who's more particular about routines at home. She likes the towels folded in thirds, not halves, and they have to go in the linen closet with the folded edge facing out. She says it looks neater, and I guess she's right, it does look like a hotel in there. But me? I'm pretty easygoing when it comes to that stuff. If I fold a towel in half, it's not the end of the world. I don't feel any kind of burning need to redo it or anything. 

Even with the caregiving stuff, the protocols I was talking about at the meeting, those are professional standards, not personal rituals. It's about keeping people safe, not some weird itch I have to scratch in my own head. When I'm at home, I'm just... well, lately I'm just sitting around worrying, like I said. But before all this, I'd just watch a little TV, maybe tinker with the lawnmower if it was acting up—it's an older Toro model, always needs a little finessing with the spark plug—or just relax on the porch. I don't have any strict routines I have to follow, no counting things, no washing my hands fifty times, nothing like that. Just a regular guy trying to get through the day, you know? Well, trying and lately failing, I suppose, given the whole administrative leave situation. But no, no rituals.
Have you been feeling anxious or worried about everyday things for more than six months?

Six months? Oh, no, no. Not at all. I mean, if you look back six months ago, things were completely fine. Actually, six months ago would have been... what, the end of summer? Early fall? Yeah, because I remember we had the big autumn festival at the senior center, and I was helping Mr. Henderson carve this giant pumpkin—well, mostly I carved it and he just pointed to where he wanted the eyes and the teeth—and I wasn't worried about anything back then. Life was just... normal. You know? I'd get up, have my oatmeal, catch the bus, do my shift, come home to Sarah. We'd watch Jeopardy! after dinner. There wasn't this heavy cloud hanging over me like there is now. 

I mean, sure, everyone worries a little bit sometimes. You worry about the electric bill going up a few bucks in the winter, or if the car is going to need new brake pads before inspection time, but just normal everyday stuff that passes. It wasn't this constant, gnawing feeling in my stomach that I can't shake. That really only started recently. Just since this whole... this whole meeting disaster and being put on administrative leave. That's when the worry really kicked into high gear, because suddenly my whole livelihood is up in the air. 

Like I was saying before, sitting at home, watching the dishes pile up in the sink, knowing I can't go in and help Mrs. Gable with her socks or take Mr. Henderson for his walk... that's what's making me anxious right now. It's the not knowing what's going to happen with my job. But if you're asking about a long-term thing, like half a year of feeling like this about just regular everyday things? No, definitely not. Before this whole mess started, I was perfectly fine, just taking things one day at a time, enjoying the routine of it all. It's really just the shock of being told you can't do your job that sets your mind spinning, you know? Not some long-term worry.
Have you found yourself talking more than usual since the incident at the staff meeting?

Talking more? Like... just talking a lot? No, I... I really don't think so. I mean, who would I even be talking to, right? With this whole administrative leave thing, I'm just stuck at the house all day by myself. 

When I was at the center, I was always talking. You have to in that line of work. You're constantly greeting the residents, asking Mrs. Gable about her grandkids—she has three, you know, two in college and one who just started middle school, plays the trombone, I think—or you're coordinating with the other aides. You're always calling down the hall, saying, "Hey, I need a hand with this transfer," or "Did someone check the thermostat in the rec room? It's freezing in there." So I was always using my voice, always chatting someone up or keeping the residents entertained. 

But now? It's just me and a quiet house. Sarah works during the day, she does data entry for a logistics company over on the east side, so she's gone from about eight to five every day. So it's literally just me. I might have the TV on for some background noise, maybe catch some old reruns of M*A*S*H or whatever happens to be on daytime cable, but it's not like I'm sitting there having conversations with the television screen. 

And when Sarah gets home... I mean, sure, we talk about what we're going to do for supper, or I might vent a little bit about how unfair this whole situation is and how stressed I am about my job, but I'm not... I'm not just babbling at her or talking her ear off. She's tired from staring at spreadsheets all day, so I try to give her some peace. If anything, I feel like I'm probably quieter than usual overall because I'm just so stuck in my own head with all this worry about the bills and my clients. And like I said before, I'm even skipping the Sunday coffee group at church, so I'm definitely not talking to them, either. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm talking more. If anything, I'm probably losing my voice from just sitting around in silence all day.
Have you noticed yourself speaking excessively or having difficulty stopping talking when you're with others?

Excessively? No, no, I wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, I know we just touched on this a second ago, but I really don't think I have any trouble stopping once I get going. It's just about having a normal back-and-forth, you know? 

Like, take Sarah and me in the evenings. When she gets home from the logistics company—she’s been doing that data entry job for, gosh, it has to be going on four years now, right after they opened that big distribution warehouse over off Route 9—we just have a regular conversation. I ask her how her day was, and she tells me about her spreadsheets or if her manager, Gary, is breathing down her neck again. Gary's always moving her deadlines up at the last minute, which really isn't fair to her, and I tell her she ought to say something to HR, but she hates making waves. But the point is, when she's talking about Gary, I sit there and I listen to her. I don't just run over her words or keep babbling about my own problems. I know how to take turns. 

It was the exact same way when I was working at the center. You have to be a good listener in personal care. If Mrs. Gable is telling me all about her grandson's middle school band schedule, I'm not going to just interrupt her and start talking about myself. That’s just plain rude. You nod, you say "Oh, that's nice," you let them finish. 

I've known people who can't stop talking, though. My Uncle Bob used to be exactly like that, especially at Thanksgiving. He’d corner you right by the buffet line, usually when you were just trying to get some mashed potatoes, and he’d talk your ear off for twenty minutes straight about the carburetor on his old Ford truck. You couldn't get a word in edgewise if you tried! But I'm definitely not like Uncle Bob. I'm just... well, I'm just trying to explain things to you clearly right now. I want to make sure you have the complete picture of what's going on with me and this whole unfair administrative leave nightmare, because if I leave out a detail, how are you supposed to understand the full situation, right? I just think it's important you know the context. But if you want me to stop talking, I can absolutely stop. I don't have any problem putting a lid on it, I just like to be thorough. So, no, definitely not excessive.
Have you often found yourself talking so much that others around you seemed annoyed or tried to interrupt you?

Annoyed? No... no, I really try to be conscious of that sort of thing. I don't think anyone's ever been annoyed by me talking. 

It's like I was saying about Sarah—she comes home from the logistics place and she's just completely wiped out from staring at a screen all day. If I was sitting there talking a mile a minute and getting on her nerves, she would absolutely tell me. She's not shy about that sort of thing at all. Like, if I'm standing in front of the TV when she's trying to watch the Final Jeopardy clue, she'll wave her hands and say, "Hey, down in front!" So if I was babbling so much that it was bothering her, she'd definitely just tell me to put a sock in it. But she doesn't. We just have our normal talks while we eat. 

And at the center, before all this administrative leave garbage happened, nobody ever tried to cut me off or walk away from me. The residents actually love it when you take the time to talk to them. So many aides just rush in, check their vitals, drop off their trays, and rush right back out into the hallway without saying two words. But I'd actually stay and converse with them. Mrs. Gable never looked annoyed, she always looked grateful for the company. 

And the other staff, too. Like Brenda, she works the front desk on the first floor. Sometimes we'd stand there by the time clock for ten, maybe fifteen minutes just shooting the breeze about the weather or her husband's gout—he gets it really bad in his big toe around the holidays—and she never once tried to interrupt me or act like she needed to get away. We just had a good back-and-forth. 

So no, I really don't think I annoy anyone with my talking. I just... I just like to make sure I'm explaining things fully, you know? Just like I'm doing right now with you. I want to make sure I'm being completely understood because this whole situation with my job is so complicated, and if I don't give you all the details, you might get the wrong idea. But I'm definitely not annoying anyone. Nobody's getting mad at me or telling me to hush.
Have you found it harder to focus on tasks or activities since the incident at the staff meeting?

Focus? Well... yeah, actually, I really have. It’s been incredibly frustrating, to be honest with you. 

Like, I’ve been trying to get through these forms they sent me in the mail. Because with this whole administrative leave situation, HR sent over this thick packet of paperwork regarding my health benefits and the union representation, and it’s just pages and pages of all this tiny legal print. So I'll sit down at the kitchen table, get a black pen out because they say it has to be black ink, and I try to just knock it out. But if I'm trying to fill out those forms, or even if I'm just trying to talk with somebody, like having a serious conversation with Sarah about our grocery budget, the slightest little thing just completely derails me. 

A door will squeak—our front screen door has this awful squeak because a storm caught it last April and bent the top hinge, I’ve been meaning to spray some WD-40 on it for months—or Sarah's phone will buzz on the counter because Gary from the logistics company is emailing her after hours again, or I'll just catch someone walking past the living room window out on the sidewalk out of the corner of my eye... and that's it. It just pulls me completely off track. 

I'll stop mid-sentence or mid-signature, get up to look at who's walking by, or I'll go over to check the phone, and then I completely forget about the paperwork or what Sarah and I were even talking about. I'll end up starting something else entirely. Like, suddenly I'm in the kitchen and I notice a spot on the counter, so I start scrubbing the grout behind the sink, and the next thing I know I'm pulling everything out of the cabinets to reorganize the Tupperware. The forms just sit there on the table, blank. I just can't seem to lock in on one thing without my attention getting yanked away by whatever just made a noise.
Have you been more active or restless than usual since the incident at the staff meeting?

Active? Restless? Well, yeah, I guess you could definitely say that. Actually, Sarah was just saying something about this the other day, because on those high-energy days—which I’ve been having a lot of lately since I’ve been stuck at home on this ridiculous leave—I just can't seem to sit down. It's like I have a motor running inside me and I have to use it. 

Take last Tuesday, for example. I woke up at, I don't know, maybe 4:30 or 5:00 in the morning? And I just felt this huge surge, like everything needed to be done right that very second. So I started cleaning out the hall closets. And I don't mean just straightening up, I mean pulling every single winter coat, every old pair of boots, all the board games we never even play—like that old Monopoly set with the missing thimble—completely out into the hallway so I could reorganize them by season and color. 

And then, right in the middle of that, I started thinking about the center. Because even though I'm not supposed to be there right now, I know their floor routines are a total mess. So I sat down at the kitchen table and started completely rewriting all the daily care checklists for the aides. The old ones are just so inefficient, they have you walking from room 12 all the way to the south supply closet just for extra linens when they should be stocked in the midway cart, you know? I filled up a whole yellow legal pad with better, color-coded checklists. 

But even doing all that wasn't enough, because then I got this amazing idea for the church. We go to First Presbyterian over on Elm, and I realized they haven't had a proper community health fair in probably a decade. So I started planning out this massive health fair—mapping out exactly where the blood pressure screening booths would go in the fellowship hall, figuring out which local pharmacies to invite to do flu shots, drawing up a schedule for guest speakers. And I felt like it had to happen immediately. Like, right then and there. So I started calling people. I was calling the pastor, I was calling the church secretary, I even called Brenda from the center to see if she wanted to run a booth. And I was making all these calls before breakfast! It was barely 6:15 in the morning and I'm leaving all these long voicemails because I just couldn't wait. I just had so much energy and so many ideas, and it all felt so incredibly urgent. Like if I didn't get the ball rolling right that second, the whole opportunity would just vanish. So, yes, I've definitely been a lot more active than usual.
Have you been having any thoughts that keep repeating in your mind and are difficult to stop?

Thoughts that keep repeating? Like... like getting a song stuck in your head, or like a broken record? No, no, I don't really get anything like that. 

I mean, I have a lot of thoughts, obviously, like I was just telling you with the church health fair and the supply closet checklists and all those big ideas. But they aren't stuck. They don't just loop over and over where I can't turn them off. If anything, it's kind of the exact opposite, you know? Like I was saying earlier, my mind is jumping from the center's floor routines to the church fellowship hall to the winter coats in the hallway. It's definitely not stuck on just one single thing. 

Like, take Sarah's brother, Mike. Now he gets stuck on things. He'll come over for Sunday dinner and he'll talk about his fantasy football team for three hours straight, just completely fixated on his draft picks and whether his tight end has a sprained ankle, and you literally cannot get him to stop thinking about it or talking about it. He just stews on it while we're trying to eat the pot roast. But me? I'm not like that at all. I just like to be thorough when I'm handling a situation. 

If I'm thinking about a problem—like how that HR department still hasn't called me back about my union representation for this whole administrative leave mess—I'll think about it, sure. I'll analyze the situation, I'll maybe write down a few bullet points on that yellow legal pad so I have my facts straight for when they finally do decide to pick up the phone. But once I've got it figured out and I've made my plan, I move on. I don't just sit there in the living room agonizing over the exact same thought all afternoon. I've got way too many other things to do, too many projects to get moving on around the house, to just sit around letting one thought bounce around in my skull all day. 

So no, I wouldn't say I have thoughts that I can't stop. I'm in complete control of what I'm thinking about, I just happen to be thinking about a lot of important things right now.
Did you have difficulty paying attention or sitting still when you were a child?

When I was a kid? No, not really. I mean, I know I was just telling you how I can't seem to focus on those HR forms right now, but back then? No, I was completely different. 

Take fourth grade, for example. I had Mrs. Higgins. Her classroom was right at the end of the hall, right next to the cafeteria, actually, so the whole room always smelled like tater tots on Thursdays and square pizza on Fridays. But anyway, I wasn't one of those kids who couldn't sit in their chair. You know the type—the ones who are always tapping their pencils on the desk, or getting up to use the pencil sharpener every five minutes just so they have an excuse to walk around the room. We had this one kid in my class, Tommy Larson, I think his name was, and he was always getting sent out to the hallway or down to the principal's office because he just physically could not stay in his seat during silent reading time. He’d literally be crawling under the desks or bothering the girls in the row next to him. 

But I wasn't like that at all. I could sit there just fine. I might have been daydreaming a little bit, sure, looking out the window at the swing sets or thinking about what I was going to do when I got home—we had this big dirt hill behind our house where my older brother and I would take our bikes and try to build these ramps out of scrap wood we found behind the hardware store—but I wasn't restless. I didn't have a motor running back then. 

I paid attention when I needed to. I could sit at my desk, do my spelling worksheets, listen to the teacher talk about state capitals... I didn't have any trouble focusing as a child. I mean, I ended up leaving high school in the tenth grade, but that wasn't because I couldn't sit still or pay attention to the chalkboard. I just kind of lost interest in the whole school thing and wanted to get out and start working and making my own money. But as a young kid? No, I was totally fine. It's really just recently, with all this ridiculous stress from the center and being stuck at home on leave, that my brain feels like it's ping-ponging all over the place. Back then, I could sit still for hours if I had to.
Have you always talked as much as you do now, or is this something that has changed recently?

Always talked this much? No, no way. Definitely not. I mean, if you asked Sarah, she’d probably tell you I’m usually the quiet one in the house. Like, normally, when we’re just sitting around in the evenings—we like to watch those home renovation shows, you know, the ones where they take a total disaster of a house and completely gut it and fix it up in like four weeks? Which, by the way, is completely unrealistic because getting the city permits alone takes months, especially if you're messing with the plumbing or knocking down load-bearing walls. But anyway, usually during those shows, I barely say two words. I just sit back in my recliner and watch. 

And it’s the same thing at work. At the center, I’m known for just putting my head down and getting the job done. When you’re a personal care aide, you really have to be a listener, not a talker. Like when I'm helping Mr. Henderson with his morning shave or getting Mrs. Gable transferred into her wheelchair, you just listen to them talk about their grandkids or what they had for breakfast in 1962 or whatever. I’m usually pretty quiet. I just do my job.

But lately? Man, lately it’s like a dam broke or something. The words just come out so fast, and I feel like I absolutely have to say them. It's just because my brain is moving so quickly with all these plans. Like I was telling you about the church health fair and the supply checklists—there’s just so much that needs to be communicated right this very second. I feel like if I don’t get it all out, if I don’t explain every single detail of how the blood pressure screening booths need to be set up exactly ten feet away from the refreshment table so there's no bottlenecking near the exit doors, people are just going to completely mess it up. 

So yeah, this talking... this is definitely new. I usually keep to myself, but right now I just have this massive urge to talk because there are just so many incredibly important things happening all at once, and nobody else seems to be moving fast enough to keep up with me unless I explain it to them from start to finish.
Have you ever had recurring, intrusive thoughts or images that you couldn't ignore, before this incident at the staff meeting?

Intrusive images? Like pictures flashing in my head that I can't push away? No, no, nothing like that. Before that whole... situation at the staff meeting—which, honestly, was completely blown out of proportion by the facility director anyway, because all I was trying to do was explain why the current protocol for the morning linen carts is incredibly inefficient and how I had figured out a much better system—but before that? My mind was perfectly clear. 

I didn't have anything forcing its way into my head. I've always been a very practical, straightforward thinker, you know? Like if I’m at work, helping Mr. Henderson with his breakfast tray, I’m just thinking about making sure his coffee isn't too hot and that he's got enough butter for his toast. I'm not having some random, uncontrollable thought popping up and distracting me. 

Or even when I'm just at home, or running errands with Sarah... like when we're at the grocery store and she's spending ten minutes pressing on every single avocado in the produce section trying to find the perfect one for guacamole, I'm just standing there with the cart thinking about the rest of the list. Bread, milk, coffee filters, maybe checking to see if they have those specific brand of paper towels we like on sale. Just normal stuff. I don't get these intrusive things you're talking about. 

I mean, my brain is moving fast *now*, sure, with all these plans and ideas I was telling you about, but I've never had things just pop into my head that I couldn't ignore or push away. So before that staff meeting, everything was completely standard. Just regular, everyday thinking. Nothing intrusive at all.
Have you always been someone who talks a lot, or is this something that has changed for you over time?

Wait, didn't you just ask me that? I feel like we just went over this a couple of minutes ago. 

But yeah, like I was saying before, it’s definitely a recent change. I’ve never been a chatterbox. I mean, think about it, if I was always talking this much, Sarah would have kicked me out of the house years ago. She likes her peace and quiet, especially after she gets off work. She works over in the billing department for that big dental practice across town, the one next to the old mall, and she is on the phone with insurance companies literally all day long, just arguing about copays and out-of-network deductibles and all that nonsense. So when she gets home, the absolute last thing she wants is someone talking her ear off. 

And normally, I'm exactly on the same page. We just eat our dinner, maybe I'll go mess around in the garage for a bit. I've got this old '98 Chevy truck I've been trying to fix up—mostly just tinkering with the carburetor, trying to get the idle right, nothing major, but I can spend four or five hours out there with the radio on and not say a single word to anybody. I like the quiet. Or at least, I usually do. 

So, no, to answer your question again, I haven't always talked this much. It’s a total 180 from my normal personality. It’s just lately, with all these ideas moving so fast in my head and nobody else stepping up to handle the logistics for the health fair, the words just... they have to come out. If I don't say it all out loud, nothing is going to get done right. But yeah, this is definitely a new thing for me.
Do you feel like you have to keep talking to relieve anxiety or discomfort?

Anxiety? Discomfort? No, no, it's not like that at all. I mean, I guess if I couldn't talk I'd feel frustrated, but it's not like I'm talking because I'm nervous or trying to make myself feel better or something. It's not like... you know when you see someone who's terrified of flying and they just start babbling to the person next to them on the airplane about their cat or what they had for lunch just to distract themselves from the fact that they're thirty thousand feet in the air in a metal tube? It's not like that. 

I don't have this nervous energy where I'm just filling the silence because I'm uncomfortable. I'm talking because there is just so much information that has to be conveyed. Like I was saying about the health fair, the logistics are incredibly complex. If you don't explain every single detail, people are going to make mistakes. Like if I don't specifically tell Pastor Dave that the extension cords for the blood pressure machines need to be taped down with the heavy-duty gaffer tape—not the cheap masking tape he always tries to buy from the dollar store, because that stuff peels right up off the linoleum the second someone steps on it—then somebody is going to trip, and then we've got a liability issue on our hands before the fair even officially opens. 

So I have to talk. I have to explain these things. It's not to relieve anxiety, it's just... it's a necessity. The words are there, the plans are there, and my brain is just firing so fast, connecting all these dots that nobody else seems to be seeing. If I don't get it out, it's not discomfort, it's just... inefficiency. It's like having a high-powered engine and trying to run it at ten miles an hour. It just doesn't make sense. I have to let it out so things get done the right way. So, no, it's definitely not about anxiety.
Do you feel like you have to keep talking to calm down or feel better?

Wait, doc, seriously, are you writing this down? Because I feel like I literally just answered this. "Anxiety, discomfort, calm down, feel better"—it's all the exact same question, isn't it? 

Like I just explained with the whole situation with Pastor Dave and the gaffer tape, it has absolutely zero to do with me needing to soothe myself or settle my nerves. I don't need to calm down. I am perfectly calm. Well, maybe not calm like I'm asleep in a hammock on a Sunday afternoon, but my mood is completely fine. I feel great, actually. Better than great. 

I don't talk like this because it's some kind of therapy for myself. I'm not venting or trying to make myself feel better. I'm directing. There's a massive difference. You see, if I sit in silence, I don't start getting the shakes or feeling upset or anything like that. The only thing that happens if I stop talking is that the entire logistical framework of this health fair completely collapses. Because, and I cannot stress this enough, nobody else is paying attention to the actual layout of the event. 

Take last year, for example—and this is exactly why I have to keep explaining things to everyone right now—last year they put the Red Cross blood donation bus right next to the inflatable bounce house that the Rotary Club rented for the kids. Do you understand how incredibly stupid that is? You've got people with needles in their arms trying to donate blood, and twenty feet away you've got a dozen screaming eight-year-olds jumping up and down, basically shaking the pavement. 

So, if I'm talking a lot, it's to prevent absolute idiocy like that from happening again. It's not so I can "feel better." I already feel fantastic because my brain is finally firing on all cylinders and I can see exactly how all these moving pieces fit together. I just need everyone else to catch up to where I'm at.
